topic: Bayes' Theorem and the Geometry of Changing Probabilistic Beliefs
target_audience: University students or advanced high school students with a basic understanding of probability

outline.topic: Bayes' Theorem and the Geometry of Changing Probabilistic Beliefs
outline.target_audience: University students or advanced high school students with a basic understanding of probability

sections.title: The Detective's Dilemma: Introducing Prior Belief
sections.content: Introduce the core concept of Bayes' Theorem not as a dry formula, but as a method for updating beliefs based on evidence. We start with a 'Prior Probability'—our best guess before seeing new data.
sections.example: A Forest Ranger finds a rare 'Cerulean Feather'. She wonders: Is the legendary Blue Phoenix nearby? Without the feather, she knows the Phoenix is rare (1% chance). This 1% is her 'Prior Belief' (P(H)).

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Unit Square as the Universal Set
sections.content: To visualize probability geometrically, we represent the entire 'Universe of Possibilities' as a 1x1 square with an area of 1. Any event is a sub-area within this square.
sections.example: Draw a square. Split it vertically: a thin sliver (1%) represents 'Phoenix is Present' (H), and the remaining 99% represents 'Phoenix is Absent' (¬H). The total area is 1.0.

sections.title: The Evidence Filter (Likelihoods)
sections.content: Introduce 'Likelihoods' as horizontal segments within our vertical strips. We ask: 'If the hypothesis were true, how likely is this evidence?' and 'If it were false, how likely is it?'
sections.example: Within the 'Phoenix' strip, color 90% of the height to represent 'Likelihood of finding a feather if Phoenix exists' (P(E|H)). In the 'No Phoenix' strip, color a tiny 5% height for 'finding a feather by fluke' (P(E|¬H)).

sections.title: The Geometry of the Intersection
sections.content: Focus on the physical overlap. The 'Evidence' (E) has occurred, so everything outside the shaded 'Evidence' area is now impossible. We highlight the intersection of 'Hypothesis' and 'Evidence'.
sections.example: The screen fades out the unshaded areas. We are left with two rectangles: A (Phoenix + Feather) and B (No Phoenix + Feather). The total area of these two rectangles is the 'Total Probability of Evidence' P(E).

sections.title: Updating the Belief: The Posterior
sections.content: Explain that the new probability is simply the ratio of the 'Success' rectangle to the 'Total Evidence' area. This is 'Normalizing' our world to the new evidence.
sections.example: Zoom into the rectangles from Section 4. The updated belief (Posterior) is: Area(Phoenix + Feather) divided by [Area(Phoenix + Feather) + Area(Fluke Feather)]. Geometrically, it's the proportion of the 'Evidence Strip' that belongs to our Hypothesis.

sections.title: Mapping Geometry to the Formula
sections.content: Overlay the standard mathematical notation of Bayes' Theorem onto the geometric shapes created in the previous steps to solidify the connection.
sections.example: Show P(H|E) = [P(H) * P(E|H)] / P(E). The numerator is the Area of the 'Target Rectangle'; the denominator is the 'Total Shaded Area'. Use color-coded labels to link the variables to the square's dimensions.

storyboard.title: The Detective's Dilemma: Introducing Prior Belief
lecture_lines: Bayes' Theorem helps us update beliefs using new evidence.
We begin with a Prior Belief before seeing data.
Imagine a Ranger seeking a rare Blue Phoenix.
animations: Display a blue feather icon (#00FFFF) and a ranger silhouette (#FFFFFF) on the left.
Show 'Prior P(H) = 1%' text in light blue (#ADD8E6) near the ranger.
Scale the '1%' text up and down to emphasize our starting guess.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Unit Square as the Universal Set
lecture_lines: We visualize all possibilities inside a unit square.
The square's total area represents a probability of one.
We split it vertically to show the Phoenix's rarity.
animations: Draw a white unit square (#FFFFFF) centered on screen.
Split the square vertically: a 1% blue strip (#0000FF) on the left.
Label the left strip 'H' and the right 99% strip 'not H' (#AAAAAA).

storyboard.title: The Evidence Filter (Likelihoods)
lecture_lines: Likelihoods describe how evidence appears under each scenario.
If the Phoenix is present, finding a feather is likely.
We shade a tall region within the Phoenix strip.
If absent, finding a feather is just a fluke.
We shade a tiny region in the non-Phoenix strip.
animations: Within the 'H' strip, shade the bottom 90% in light blue (#ADD8E6).
Within the 'not H' strip, shade the bottom 5% in yellow (#FFFF00).
Label the shaded areas 'P(E|H)' and 'P(E|not H)' respectively.

storyboard.title: The Geometry of the Intersection
lecture_lines: Evidence has occurred, so only shaded areas remain possible.
We focus on the intersection of hypothesis and evidence.
These two rectangles represent our new world of possibilities.
animations: Fade out all unshaded areas from the unit square.
Highlight the two remaining shaded rectangles: the tall blue one and the tiny yellow one.
Pulse both rectangles to show they represent the total evidence P(E).

storyboard.title: Updating the Belief: The Posterior
lecture_lines: The new probability is the ratio of these areas.
We compare the Phoenix rectangle to the total evidence.
This process 'normalizes' our belief to the new evidence.
Geometrically, it is the Phoenix portion of the evidence.
Our updated belief is called the Posterior Probability.
animations: Move the blue rectangle to the top and the yellow one below it.
Draw a white bracket (#FFFFFF) encompassing both to represent 'Total Evidence'.
Scale the blue rectangle to fill its proportion of the total stack.

storyboard.title: Mapping Geometry to the Formula
lecture_lines: Now let's map these shapes to the standard formula.
The numerator is the area of our target rectangle.
The denominator is the sum of all shaded areas.
Color-coded labels link the formula to the square's geometry.
Bayes' Theorem turns visual proportions into precise mathematical values.
animations: Write P(H|E) = [P(H) * P(E|H)] / P(E) in white (#FFFFFF).
Highlight 'P(H) * P(E|H)' and draw an arrow to the blue rectangle area.
Highlight 'P(E)' and draw an arrow to the sum of both rectangle areas.
